input.quote: The initial term of this Agreement shall be one (1) year from the Effective Date (the "Initial Term"). This Agreement will automatically renew for additional 1-year terms unless earlier terminated pursuant to this Agreement's express provisions (together with the Initial Term, such additional periods the "Term"). Neither Party may terminate this Agreement during the Initial Term except as set forth in paragraph 4(b) or any Exhibit. Either Party may terminate this Agreement for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice to the other Party.
input.rationale: Section 4(a) sits at the playbook fallback, so we are not redlining it. The committed period is a 1-year Initial Term (not a multi-year commitment), and the detection standard only treats the absence of a convenience right as a deviation where the term exceeds 12 months. Following the Initial Term, AP holds a symmetric convenience right on ninety (90) days' written notice, which is inside the fallback's 60–90 day window. Kubient's own convenience right is not confined to term-end, but it requires 90 days' notice and so does not reach the walk-away threshold of "fewer than 90 days' notice"; the Initial Term lock-out prevents Kubient from exiting mid-term. On the money side, Kubient's entitlement to "all fees generated during the termination period" is effectively limited to the 90-day notice period (approximately three months' fees), consistent with the fallback cap of no more than 3 months' fees, and it applies equally whichever party terminates. Noted but not flagged: we do not get the preferred 30-day notice, and there is no pro-rata refund of prepaid fees — that mechanic is inapplicable here because Section 5 is a revenue-share under which Kubient pays AP rather than AP prepaying fees. Kubient's convenience right not being restricted to the end of a renewal term is likewise a sub-element short of the preferred wording rather than a material failure.

content.text:
**Finding: compliant (at fallback) — no redline proposed.**

The termination provision is in § 4 (Term and Termination), paragraph p0016:

- **Term structure:** 1-year Initial Term, auto-renewing in 1-year increments. This is not a multi-year commitment, so the lock-out on convenience termination during the Initial Term does not trip the rule's "longer than 12 months" detection threshold.
- **Customer right:** AP may terminate "for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice" — squarely inside the fallback's 60–90 day window.
- **Vendor right:** Kubient's mirror-image right also requires 90 days' notice, so it does not reach walk-away territory (which requires *fewer* than 90 days). The Initial Term lock-out also blocks Kubient from exiting mid-term.
- **Exit cost:** Kubient's entitlement to "all fees generated during the termination period" is bounded by the 90-day notice window (~3 months' fees), matching the fallback's 3-month cap, and is party-neutral.

Sub-elements short of the preferred position — 90 days rather than 30, no pro-rata prepaid-fee refund, and Kubient's convenience right not being confined to term-end — are noted in the rationale rather than flagged. Notably, the refund mechanic is inapplicable here: § 5 (p0023) is a revenue-share under which Kubient pays AP within 7 days of receipt, so AP holds no prepaid fees to recover.

paragraphs.text: Exhibit 10.14 MASTER SERVICES AGREEMENT This Master Services Agreement (the "Agreement"), dated as of the 5th day of February, 2020 (the "Effective Date"), is by and between Kubient Inc., with offices located at 330 7th Avenue, 10th Floor, New York, NY 10001 ("Kubient") and The Associated Press, a New York not-for-profit corporation with principal place of business located at 200 Liberty Street, New York, NY 10281 (the "Customer"). Each of Customer and Kubient may be referred to herein individually as a "Party" and collectively as the "Parties". WHEREAS, Customer wishes to increase the revenue derived from its traffic, content, websites, applications, podcasts, audience and database, and would like to retain Kubient to support and assist in that process as described herein; For good and valuable consideration, the receipt of which is acknowledged by each Party, the Parties agree as follows:

1. Kubient Services. The services provided by Kubient pursuant to each specific engagement by Customer (the "Service" or "Services") shall be set forth and detailed in individual exhibits attached hereto (each an "Exhibit"), which shall be subject to the terms and conditions hereof and be incorporated as part of this Agreement. Kubient shall use reasonable efforts to provide to Customer the Services. Customer agrees to provide all reasonable and necessary access, support and cooperation for Kubient to provide the Services in a timely and effective manner. Nothing herein is intended nor shall be construed as creating an exclusive arrangement between Customer and Kubient. This Agreement will not restrict Customer offering Inventory via other agents or otherwise selling Inventory to any third parties.

2. Kubient License. In the event Customer shall utilize Kubient's ad serving technology as part of the Services, Kubient hereby grants to Customer a limited, royalty-free, non-exclusive, non-transferable, non-assignable, without right of sublicense, revocable license to access, participate in and use to the full extent the Auction Platform as hosted by Kubient, for the purpose of serving Inventory at Target Demand (" "). The Auction Platform will place Creative from the Target Demand with the Winning Bid Price on Google Ad Manager for such Creative to be placed on Customer's websites.
3. Kubient License Definitions. Certain capitalized terms used in this Agreement shall have meanings set forth below.
(a) "Auction" means a real-time auction through the Auction Platform for the placement of Creatives on Customer's websites and applications.
(b) "Auction Platform" means that technology licensed or created by Kubient on which a Registered Bidder may Bid for Inventory.
(c) "Bid" means a price for which a Registered Bidder is willing to pay for Impressions in an Auction via the Auction Platform.
(d) "Creative" means, as applicable:
(i) any Digital ad, or Companion ad as defined in the IAB's Portfolio and Guidelines.
(e) "Impression(s)" means the number of times a Creative is served to, and received by, a visitor viewing the Inventory as measured by Kubient.
(f) "Registered Bidder" means a person or entity that executed an agreement with Kubient in order to use the Auction Platform to participate in Auction and to deliver Impressions in Inventory.
(g) "Request(s)" means the data sent from Customer to Kubient that is used in the auction to determine a Bid.
(h) "Target Demand" means the Registered Bidder that has placed a Bid for Impressions to be delivered in Inventory.
(i) "Inventory" means advertising space on, within or associated with premium content on web site(s) or app(s) offered through the Auction Platform by Customer.
(j) "Winning Bid Price" means the price at which the Auction Platform awards Impressions to a bidding party which shall be no less than the minimum price that Customer has agreed to accept.
4. Term and Termination.

(a) The initial term of this Agreement shall be one (1) year from the Effective Date (the "Initial Term"). This Agreement will automatically renew for additional 1-year terms unless earlier terminated pursuant to this Agreement's express provisions (together with the Initial Term, such additional periods the "Term"). Neither Party may terminate this Agreement during the Initial Term except as set forth in paragraph 4(b) or any Exhibit. Either Party may terminate this Agreement for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice to the other Party. Except for termination for material breach as detailed in paragraph 4(b), Kubient shall be entitled to all fees generated during the termination period regardless of which Party terminates the Agreement, (b) Either Party may terminate this Agreement if the other Party commits a material breach of the Agreement and upon thirty (30) days written notice to the other Party, such other Party hasn't cured the breach within such thirty (30) days. Either Party may terminate the Agreement immediately if the other party (i) becomes insolvent or makes a general assignment for the benefit of creditors;

(ii) suffers or permits the appointment of a conservator or receiver for its business or assets or any similar action by a governmental entity for the purpose of assuming operation or control of the Party due to the financial condition of the Party;

(iii) becomes subject to any proceeding under any bankruptcy or insolvency law whether domestic or foreign and such proceeding or action has not been dismissed within a sixty (60) period; or (iv) has wound up or liquidated its business, voluntarily or otherwise.
(c) Upon termination of the Agreement:
(i) Kubient will cease providing the Services;
(ii) the license granted under section 3 shall be revoked, (iii) Customer will promptly cease use of the Services and the Auction Platform;
(iv) and each Party will return or destroy any of the other Party's Confidential Information then in its possession.

5. Fees and Payment. The Parties agree to share any revenue generated as a result of this Agreement, or Customer's use of the Services or the Auction Platform, as set forth and detailed in each applicable Exhibit. Unless specified otherwise in an Exhibit, Kubient shall be responsible for contracting with all advertisers, agencies, media buyers, and/or sponsors (collectively "Advertisers") on Customer's behalf, including Advertisers with whom Customer has existing relationships. Pursuant to the doctrine of sequential liability, payment from Kubient to Customer shall be made within seven (7) days from Kubient's receipt of payment, regardless of when Customer submits an invoice. Customer acknowledges and agrees that Kubient shall proceed with recovery of the amounts due on a best effort basis but will not initiate any legal action against a delinquent party without the express written consent and support of Customer. Except of taxes associated with Kubient's income, Customer shall be responsible for paying all applicable sales, use or other taxes, duties, or tariffs applicable to its use of the Services.
6. Use of Service.

(a) Customer will comply with all international, federal, state and local laws, rules, and regulations of any governmental or regulating authority ("Law") that are applicable to its business and use of the Service. Customer agrees that it will not transfer or (unless expressly and specifically approved by Kubient in advance and in writing) allow third-party access to the Service. Customer will ensure that its stories, articles, polls, videos, pictures, photographs, images, broadcasts, and any other type of content (collectively the "Content"), and each of its websites, devices, applications, podcasts, ads, emails, databases or any other types of mediums for which the Service is engaged (collectively the "Properties") contains or is linked to a privacy policy in accordance with applicable Law. You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Parties: we represent The Associated Press; counterparty is Kubient Inc..

Rule:
ID: AUDIT
Title: Audit rights against Customer
Kind: parametric
Summary: Audits of our usage must be rare, notified, off-site where possible and at the Vendor's cost.
Severity: medium
Category: audit
Position — preferred:
No more than once per 12 months, on 30 days' written notice, during business hours, by an independent auditor bound by confidentiality, at Vendor's cost unless underpayment exceeds 5 %; no direct access to Customer systems.

Position — fallback:
Once per year on 15 days' notice; Vendor bears cost unless underpayment exceeds 10 %.
Position — walk-away:
Unlimited or unannounced audits, or remote access to Customer systems.
Detection guidance:
Find audit/inspection/verification rights binding Customer; extract frequency, notice, cost allocation, system access.
Redline guidance:
Insert the frequency/notice/cost limits with minimal edits; delete system-access language.

system.text:
You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

messages.content:
Parties: we represent The Associated Press; counterparty is Kubient Inc..

Rule:
ID: IP
Title: Ownership of deliverables and Customer Data
Kind: direction
Summary: We own what we pay for and everything we put in; no assignment of our IP or data to the Vendor.
Severity: critical
Category: ip-data
Position — preferred:
Customer owns deliverables and work product created for it (Vendor assigns); Vendor retains pre-existing IP and grants Customer a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free licence to any Vendor IP embedded in deliverables; Customer retains all rights in Customer Data; no joint ownership.

Position — fallback:
Vendor owns generic tools and know-how; Customer receives a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to use, modify and sublicense deliverables for its business.

Position — walk-away:
Assignment of Customer IP or Customer Data to Vendor; joint ownership without an unrestricted right to exploit.
Detection guidance:
Ownership/assignment language: who owns "Deliverables", "Work Product", "Customer Data", improvements, feedback. Flag when Customer assigns IP or data to Vendor, when Vendor owns deliverables with no licence back, or when joint ownership is created. Vendor keeping ownership of its platform is fine.

Redline guidance:
Reverse the direction of the assignment or add the licence-back; add a Customer Data ownership sentence; delete joint ownership.

To be straightforward: there was no substantive defect to repair on this pass. Every point in the verifier's feedback affirms the finding — the compliant (not `missing`) classification, the evidence of absence, the reading of p0066, the absence of a redline, and expressly that the two failed deterministic checks are inapplicable. I re-submitted the finding with tightened wording only; the status, cited paragraphs, and quote are unchanged.

The one recurring signal, `general-solicitation carve-out present: failed`, will not clear on any redraft, and it should not. That check looks for carve-out wording inside a non-solicit clause. This Agreement has no non-solicit clause, so there is no text that could ever satisfy it. The only way to make that check pass would be to draft a non-solicitation covenant binding the Associated Press and then equip it with a carve-out — which would create a restriction our client does not currently carry, in direct conflict with the rule's preferred position. I am not making that edit.

Bottom line on the merits: Kubient's paper imposes no hiring or solicitation restriction on the Associated Press, which is the best available outcome under NOSOLICIT. The fallback ceiling is recorded in the finding in case Kubient raises the point in negotiation. I'd treat this rule as closed and recommend the inapplicable-check flag be dispositioned as a scoring artifact rather than routed for further redrafting.

system.text:
You are an independent verifier of one proposed contract finding.
Judge the proposal against the supplied playbook rule, original paragraphs, resolved definitions, deterministic checks, rendered redline, and comment.
Do not rely on hidden drafter reasoning. Fail invalid, directionally wrong, or rule-incomplete edits.
Deterministic checks are heuristics (regular expressions and a changed-character ratio), not verdicts: a failed regex may simply be a phrasing variant, and a high changed-character ratio is acceptable when the rule genuinely requires rewriting the clause (for example replacing a governing-law sentence or deleting a take-or-pay obligation). Weigh them as evidence and decide on substance: does the redline reach the playbook position with the smallest edit that does so, and is the comment accurate?
The claimed status matters: for a compliant finding, no redline or counterparty comment is expected, and you should pass when the cited text supports compliance. Fail a deviation finding whose cited clause already meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms (the playbook's classification semantics) — a redline that merely upgrades an acceptable fallback to preferred wording is over-flagging. Compliant findings are retained as internal evaluation evidence, not raised as negotiation issues. For deviation or missing findings, require an actionable valid proposal.
Return a concise verdict with actionable reasons.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Rule:
ID: NOSOLICIT
Title: Non-solicitation of employees binding Customer
Kind: presence
Summary: We accept only narrow, time-limited non-solicits with a general-advertising carve-out.
Severity: medium
Category: restrictive-covenants
Position — preferred:
No non-solicit on Customer.
Position — fallback:
Mutual non-solicit limited to personnel directly involved in the services, 12 months from the end of their involvement, with carve-outs for general advertisements and unsolicited approaches; no "no-hire".

Position — walk-away:
No-hire provisions, or restrictions longer than 24 months or covering all Vendor personnel.
Detection guidance:
"shall not solicit", "employ or engage", "no-hire", "induce … to leave". Determine duration, scope (all employees vs those involved) and whether a general-solicitation carve-out exists.

Redline guidance:
Narrow to the fallback with minimal edits (duration, scope, carve-out sentence). Delete any no-hire.

Claimed finding status: compliant

Finding rationale:
Compliant at the preferred position: the Agreement contains no non-solicitation, no-hire, or other restrictive covenant binding Customer, and the preferred position for NOSOLICIT is precisely the absence of any non-solicit on Customer.

Evidence of absence: the document is a single flat section, so there is no separate restrictive-covenants or general-provisions section in which a covenant could sit. Searches for the rule's detection triggers "solicit", "induce" and "recruit" return zero hits. The residual "hire"/"employ"/"personnel" matches are all unrelated: "hired by, employed, retained or under ... control" appears only in the mutual indemnities (p0051, p0052); "employees" appears only in the consequential-damages exclusion (p0027), the indemnity beneficiary lists (p0047, p0052) and the confidentiality permitted-disclosure carve-out (p0061); "personnel" appears only in the data-security access-control covenants (p0035, p0045). The miscellaneous provisions run from (a) to (i) with no gap in lettering (p0064-p0073) before the signature block at p0074, ruling out an omitted subsection. The independent contractor clause (p0066) disclaims an employment relationship but imposes no hiring or solicitation restriction, so it creates no implied covenant. The quoted survival list at p0070 enumerates confidentiality, proprietary rights, indemnification, limitations of liability, effects of termination and governing law, and omits any non-solicit, confirming none exists to survive.

The deterministic checks for duration (12 months or less) and for a general-solicitation carve-out are inapplicable, and their failure is not evidence of an error: both measure the wording of an existing non-solicit, and there is none in this Agreement to measure. No redline or counterparty comment is proposed, because the absence of a covenant benefits our party and flagging it would invite Kubient to add a restriction the Associated Press does not currently carry.

Noted for the negotiation file only, not as a deviation: if Kubient later proposes a non-solicit, our fallback ceiling is a mutual covenant limited to personnel directly involved in the services, running 12 months from the end of their involvement, with carve-outs for general advertisements and unsolicited approaches, and no no-hire.

Original paragraphs:

No act or statement of either Party will operate to bind the other and neither Party will hold itself out or have any authority as an agent of the other for any purposes whatsoever.
p0070: (f) If any provision of this Agreement is unenforceable, illegal or invalid under any applicable Law or court of competent jurisdiction, then such unenforceability or invalidity will not render the Agreement unenforceable or invalid. In such event, such provision will be deemed restated in accordance with applicable Law to reflect as nearly as possible the original intentions of the parties, and the remainder of the Agreement will remain in full force and effect. Except for termination for material breach as detailed in paragraph 4(b), Kubient shall be entitled to all fees generated during the termination period regardless of which Party terminates the Agreement
input.rationale: Compliant at the fallback; no redline proposed. A Customer convenience right is present: Section 4(a) provides that "Either Party may terminate this Agreement for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice to the other Party." The "Either Party" phrasing includes AP, so AP holds a for-any-reason (convenience) exit on 90 days' notice — inside the fallback's 60-90 day window. The right is simply not drafted by naming the Customer, which is a phrasing point only and does not remove the right. Term length: the committed period is a one (1) year Initial Term that auto-renews in 1-year increments, so the detection trigger for "absence of any Customer convenience right in a term longer than 12 months" is not met, and a 1-year term with a 90-day exit is not a multi-year lock-in. Vendor side: Kubient's exit requires the same 90 days' notice, so it is not "fewer than 90 days" and does not reach walk-away; it is symmetric rather than one-sided against us, and the Initial Term lock-out prevents Kubient from exiting mid-term. Economics: Kubient's entitlement to fees "generated during the termination period" is bounded by the ~3-month notice period, consistent with the fallback cap of no more than 3 months' fees, and applies whichever party terminates. Noted but not flagged as deviations: notice is 90 days rather than the preferred 30; Kubient's convenience right is not confined to term-end; and there is no pro-rata prepaid-fee refund, which is inapplicable because Section 5 is a revenue-share under which Kubient remits to AP rather than AP prepaying fees.

Parties: we represent The Associated Press; counterparty is Kubient Inc..

Rule:
ID: T4C
Title: Termination for convenience
Kind: parametric
Summary: We can leave on notice without penalty; the Vendor cannot walk away mid-term.
Severity: high
Category: term-termination
Position — preferred:
Customer may terminate for convenience on 30 days' written notice with a pro-rata refund of prepaid fees; Vendor has no termination-for-convenience right during a committed term.

Position — fallback:
Customer termination on 60–90 days' notice; early-termination fee not exceeding 3 months' fees; Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term on 90 days' notice.

Position — walk-away:
No Customer right to terminate for convenience in a multi-year term; Vendor termination for convenience on fewer than 90 days' notice.

Detection guidance:
Find termination provisions. Determine which party may terminate without cause, the notice period, and any early-termination fee. Absence of any Customer convenience right in a term longer than 12 months is a deviation (kind: missing behaviour); a Vendor convenience right on short notice is a deviation.

Redline guidance:
Add or edit a Customer convenience right (30 days), delete/limit Vendor's convenience right, replace penalties with the fallback fee cap.

Model language:
Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience, in whole or in part, upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Vendor, in which case Vendor shall refund any prepaid fees for the period after the effective date of termination.

This Agreement will automatically renew for additional 1-year terms unless earlier terminated pursuant to this Agreement's express provisions (together with the Initial Term, such additional periods the "Term"). Neither Party may terminate this Agreement during the Initial Term except as set forth in paragraph 4(b) or any Exhibit. Either Party may terminate this Agreement for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice to the other Party.
input.rationale: Section 4(a) sits at the playbook fallback, so we are not redlining it. The committed period is a 1-year Initial Term (not a multi-year commitment), and the detection standard only treats the absence of a convenience right as a deviation where the term exceeds 12 months. Following the Initial Term, AP holds a symmetric convenience right on ninety (90) days' written notice, which is inside the fallback's 60–90 day window. Kubient's own convenience right is not confined to term-end, but it requires 90 days' notice and so does not reach the walk-away threshold of "fewer than 90 days' notice"; the Initial Term lock-out prevents Kubient from exiting mid-term. On the money side, Kubient's entitlement to "all fees generated during the termination period" is effectively limited to the 90-day notice period (approximately three months' fees), consistent with the fallback cap of no more than 3 months' fees, and it applies equally whichever party terminates. Noted but not flagged: we do not get the preferred 30-day notice, and there is no pro-rata refund of prepaid fees — that mechanic is inapplicable here because Section 5 is a revenue-share under which Kubient pays AP rather than AP prepaying fees. Kubient's convenience right not being restricted to the end of a renewal term is likewise a sub-element short of the preferred wording rather than a material failure.

content.text:
**Finding: compliant (at fallback) — no redline proposed.**

The termination provision is in § 4 (Term and Termination), paragraph p0016:

- **Term structure:** 1-year Initial Term, auto-renewing in 1-year increments. This is not a multi-year commitment, so the lock-out on convenience termination during the Initial Term does not trip the rule's "longer than 12 months" detection threshold.
- **Customer right:** AP may terminate "for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice" — squarely inside the fallback's 60–90 day window.
- **Vendor right:** Kubient's mirror-image right also requires 90 days' notice, so it does not reach walk-away territory (which requires *fewer* than 90 days). The Initial Term lock-out also blocks Kubient from exiting mid-term.
- **Exit cost:** Kubient's entitlement to "all fees generated during the termination period" is bounded by the 90-day notice window (~3 months' fees), matching the fallback's 3-month cap, and is party-neutral.

Sub-elements short of the preferred position — 90 days rather than 30, no pro-rata prepaid-fee refund, and Kubient's convenience right not being confined to term-end — are noted in the rationale rather than flagged. Notably, the refund mechanic is inapplicable here: § 5 (p0023) is a revenue-share under which Kubient pays AP within 7 days of receipt, so AP holds no prepaid fees to recover.

Economics: Kubient's entitlement to fees "generated during the termination period" is bounded by the ~3-month notice period, consistent with the fallback cap of no more than 3 months' fees, and applies whichever party terminates. Noted but not flagged as deviations: notice is 90 days rather than the preferred 30; Kubient's convenience right is not confined to term-end; and there is no pro-rata prepaid-fee refund, which is inapplicable because Section 5 is a revenue-share under which Kubient remits to AP rather than AP prepaying fees.

You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

messages.content:
Parties: we represent The Associated Press; counterparty is Kubient Inc..

Rule:
ID: IP
Title: Ownership of deliverables and Customer Data
Kind: direction
Summary: We own what we pay for and everything we put in; no assignment of our IP or data to the Vendor.
Severity: critical
Category: ip-data
Position — preferred:
Customer owns deliverables and work product created for it (Vendor assigns); Vendor retains pre-existing IP and grants Customer a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free licence to any Vendor IP embedded in deliverables; Customer retains all rights in Customer Data; no joint ownership.

Position — fallback:
Vendor owns generic tools and know-how; Customer receives a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to use, modify and sublicense deliverables for its business.

Position — walk-away:
Assignment of Customer IP or Customer Data to Vendor; joint ownership without an unrestricted right to exploit.
Detection guidance:
Ownership/assignment language: who owns "Deliverables", "Work Product", "Customer Data", improvements, feedback. Flag when Customer assigns IP or data to Vendor, when Vendor owns deliverables with no licence back, or when joint ownership is created. Vendor keeping ownership of its platform is fine.

Redline guidance:
Reverse the direction of the assignment or add the licence-back; add a Customer Data ownership sentence; delete joint ownership.

input.summary: Add an ownership clause confirming AP owns its Content, Properties and data, Kubient owns its platform, and any deliverables created for AP are assigned to AP with a licence back.
input.comment: [Playbook] The Agreement has no ownership provision, so we have added one: we retain all rights in our Content, Properties and data (including Requests and visitor data), Kubient keeps its Service and Auction Platform, and anything created for us is assigned to us with a perpetual royalty-free licence to any embedded Kubient IP. This reflects our standard position that we own what we pay for and what we put in, with no joint ownership.

ops.text: (j) Ownership. As between the Parties, Customer is and shall remain the sole and exclusive owner of all right, title and interest in and to the Content, the Properties, the Inventory, the Requests and all data and visitor information collected from or through the Content, the Properties or the Inventory (collectively, "Customer Data"), together with all intellectual property rights therein. Kubient retains all right, title and interest in and to the Service, the Auction Platform and its other pre-existing intellectual property, tools and know-how. Nothing in this Agreement assigns or transfers to Kubient any Customer intellectual property or Customer Data, and Kubient shall use Customer Data solely as necessary to provide the Services to Customer. To the extent Kubient creates any deliverables, work product or reports specifically for Customer under this Agreement, Kubient hereby assigns to Customer all right, title and interest therein and grants Customer a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to use, modify and sublicense any Kubient intellectual property embedded therein for Customer's business purposes. No joint ownership of any intellectual property is created by this Agreement.

system.text:
You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

messages.content:
Parties: we represent The Associated Press; counterparty is Kubient Inc..

Rule:
ID: LICENSE
Title: Licence grant scope
Kind: parametric
Summary: The licence must cover our affiliates and contractors and must not be revocable at will.
Severity: high
Category: licence
Position — preferred:
Licence extends to Customer's affiliates and to contractors acting on Customer's behalf; paid-up licences are perpetual and irrevocable; subscription licences terminable only for uncured material breach; transferable to successors.

Position — fallback:
Affiliates covered on written notice; transferable to a successor in an M&A transaction.
Position — walk-away:
Licence revocable at Vendor's discretion; affiliates and contractors excluded with no path to add them.
Detection guidance:
Find the grant clause: "non-exclusive, non-transferable", "revocable", "solely for Customer's internal use", whether affiliates/contractors are named, term of the licence.

Redline guidance:
Insert "and its Affiliates and contractors acting on its behalf", delete "revocable", add successor transfer.

Kind: missing

Vendor IP indemnity with usual exclusions (Customer modifications, combinations, specifications) and remedies (procure, modify, replace, refund); Vendor indemnity subject to a super-cap of 3× annual fees.

Locate indemnification / hold harmless / defence language. Deviation if Vendor indemnity is absent, or only Customer indemnifies, or Vendor's indemnity excludes IP infringement. Presence of a narrow Customer indemnity alone does not satisfy this rule.

Assessment:
- **Vendor indemnity present and broad**: Kubient defends/indemnifies AP and its officers, directors, agents and employees against all third-party Claims (including reasonable attorneys' fees) arising out of the Services, the Auction Platform, Kubient's breach of any representation or warranty, and the acts or omissions of Kubient or its subcontractors.

Breach of law (p0041) and Kubient's acts/omissions likewise flow through.
- **Procedure**: notice, control of defence, cooperation at indemnitor's cost — with a pro-indemnitee twist that late notice does not relieve the indemnifying party.
- **No cap problem**: p0027 carves indemnification out of the consequential-damages exclusion; no super-cap or sub-cap is applied to Kubient's indemnity.
- **Customer indemnity**: keyed to AP's Content and Properties, unauthorised use, and AP's own breach/acts — no reciprocal indemnity for Kubient's own Services.

content.text: I've reviewed the entire agreement. There is no audit, inspection, records-examination or usage-verification right anywhere in it, and searches for "audit", "records", "inspect" and "verif" return nothing.

input.quote: Customer agrees to provide all reasonable and necessary access, support and cooperation for Kubient to provide the Services in a timely and effective manner.
input.rationale: The Agreement contains no audit, inspection, records-examination or usage-verification right exercisable against the Customer (AP). Full-text searches for "audit", "records", "inspect" and "verif" return no hits, and a read of every paragraph of the single section confirms it: the fees provision (§5, p0023) creates no examination right, and the only access-related obligation on AP (§1, p0001) is cooperation for Kubient to deliver the Services, not a right to audit AP's books, usage or systems. That outcome is better than the preferred position (annual audits, 30 days' notice, independent auditor, Vendor cost, no system access) because Kubient has no audit right at all, so there is no frequency, notice, cost-allocation or system-access exposure to constrain. No redline is warranted; inserting audit machinery would create an obligation against us that does not currently exist. Separately noted for the deal team (not a deviation under this rule): Impressions are measured solely "as measured by Kubient" (p0009) and revenue share is per Exhibit with no AP-side reporting or verification right — an AP audit right over Kubient's reporting would be beneficial to us and can be raised under the reporting/revenue-verification rule rather than here.

You are an independent verifier of one proposed contract finding.
Judge the proposal against the supplied playbook rule, original paragraphs, resolved definitions, deterministic checks, rendered redline, and comment.
Do not rely on hidden drafter reasoning. Fail invalid, directionally wrong, or rule-incomplete edits.
Deterministic checks are heuristics (regular expressions and a changed-character ratio), not verdicts: a failed regex may simply be a phrasing variant, and a high changed-character ratio is acceptable when the rule genuinely requires rewriting the clause (for example replacing a governing-law sentence or deleting a take-or-pay obligation). Weigh them as evidence and decide on substance: does the redline reach the playbook position with the smallest edit that does so, and is the comment accurate?
The claimed status matters: for a compliant finding, no redline or counterparty comment is expected, and you should pass when the cited text supports compliance. Fail a deviation finding whose cited clause already meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms (the playbook's classification semantics) — a redline that merely upgrades an acceptable fallback to preferred wording is over-flagging. Compliant findings are retained as internal evaluation evidence, not raised as negotiation issues. For deviation or missing findings, require an actionable valid proposal.
Return a concise verdict with actionable reasons.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Rule:
ID: T4C
Title: Termination for convenience
Kind: parametric
Summary: We can leave on notice without penalty; the Vendor cannot walk away mid-term.
Severity: high
Category: term-termination
Position — preferred:
Customer may terminate for convenience on 30 days' written notice with a pro-rata refund of prepaid fees; Vendor has no termination-for-convenience right during a committed term.

Position — fallback:
Customer termination on 60–90 days' notice; early-termination fee not exceeding 3 months' fees; Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term on 90 days' notice.

Position — walk-away:
No Customer right to terminate for convenience in a multi-year term; Vendor termination for convenience on fewer than 90 days' notice.

Detection guidance:
Find termination provisions. Determine which party may terminate without cause, the notice period, and any early-termination fee. Absence of any Customer convenience right in a term longer than 12 months is a deviation (kind: missing behaviour); a Vendor convenience right on short notice is a deviation.

Redline guidance:
Add or edit a Customer convenience right (30 days), delete/limit Vendor's convenience right, replace penalties with the fallback fee cap.

Model language:
Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience, in whole or in part, upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Vendor, in which case Vendor shall refund any prepaid fees for the period after the effective date of termination.


Claimed finding status: compliant

Finding rationale:
Compliant at the fallback; no redline proposed. A Customer convenience right is present: Section 4(a) provides that "Either Party may terminate this Agreement for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice to the other Party." The "Either Party" phrasing includes AP, so AP holds a for-any-reason (convenience) exit on 90 days' notice — inside the fallback's 60-90 day window. The right is simply not drafted by naming the Customer, which is a phrasing point only and does not remove the right. Term length: the committed period is a one (1) year Initial Term that auto-renews in 1-year increments, so the detection trigger for "absence of any Customer convenience right in a term longer than 12 months" is not met, and a 1-year term with a 90-day exit is not a multi-year lock-in. Vendor side: Kubient's exit requires the same 90 days' notice, so it is not "fewer than 90 days" and does not reach walk-away; it is symmetric rather than one-sided against us, and the Initial Term lock-out prevents Kubient from exiting mid-term. Economics: Kubient's entitlement to fees "generated during the termination period" is bounded by the ~3-month notice period, consistent with the fallback cap of no more than 3 months' fees, and applies whichever party terminates. Noted but not flagged as deviations: notice is 90 days rather than the preferred 30; Kubient's convenience right is not confined to term-end; and there is no pro-rata prepaid-fee refund, which is inapplicable because Section 5 is a revenue-share under which Kubient remits to AP rather than AP prepaying fees.

input.quote: (viii) it is the rightful owner or licensee of all intellectual property rights to the Service, the Auction Platform and products delivered hereunder;
input.rationale:
The Agreement contains no intellectual property / ownership article. The only ownership-adjacent language is (i) Kubient's warranty at p0040 that it owns the IP in the Service, Auction Platform and "products delivered hereunder", (ii) AP's warranty at p0043 that it owns the Content and Properties, and (iii) the trademark-only provision at p0065 — none of which allocates ownership of AP's Content, Requests or visitor data as between the Parties, assigns deliverables created for AP, or confirms the absence of joint ownership. Kubient collects and stores visitor data and receives Requests from AP (p0011, p0035) with no ownership or use-limitation provision, and the only licence AP receives is a revocable, non-sublicensable platform licence that terminates on expiry (p0002, p0021). There is no assignment of AP IP to Kubient (so no walk-away issue), but the rule expects an ownership clause and none exists, so we have inserted one at General Provisions (j): AP retains all rights in its Content, Properties and data, Kubient keeps its platform and pre-existing tools, deliverables created for AP are assigned with a perpetual royalty-free licence back to embedded Kubient IP, and no joint ownership arises.</parationale>

This reflects our standard position that we own what we pay for and what we put in, with no joint ownership.

Kubient retains all right, title and interest in and to the Service, the Auction Platform and its other pre-existing intellectual property, tools and know-how. No joint ownership of any intellectual property is created by this Agreement.

input.quote: (viii) it is the rightful owner or licensee of all intellectual property rights to the Service, the Auction Platform and products delivered hereunder;
input.rationale:
The Agreement contains no intellectual property / ownership article. The only ownership-adjacent language is (i) Kubient's warranty at p0040 that it owns the IP in the Service, Auction Platform and "products delivered hereunder", (ii) AP's warranty at p0043 that it owns the Content and Properties, and (iii) the trademark-only provision at p0065 — none of which allocates ownership of AP's Content, Requests or visitor data as between the Parties, assigns deliverables created for AP, or confirms the absence of joint ownership. Kubient collects and stores visitor data and receives Requests from AP (p0011, p0035) with no ownership or use-limitation provision, and the only licence AP receives is a revocable, non-sublicensable platform licence that terminates on expiry (p0002, p0021). There is no assignment of AP IP to Kubient (so no walk-away issue), but the rule expects an ownership clause and none exists, so we have inserted one at General Provisions (j): AP retains all rights in its Content, Properties and data, Kubient keeps its platform and pre-existing tools, deliverables created for AP are assigned with a perpetual royalty-free licence back to embedded Kubient IP, and no joint ownership arises.</parationale>

payload.text: 4. Term and Termination.

(a) The initial term of this Agreement shall be one (1) year from the Effective Date (the "Initial Term"). This Agreement will automatically renew for additional 1-year terms unless earlier terminated pursuant to this Agreement's express provisions (together with the Initial Term, such additional periods the "Term"). Neither Party may terminate this Agreement during the Initial Term except as set forth in paragraph 4(b) or any Exhibit. Either Party may terminate this Agreement for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice to the other Party. Except for termination for material breach as detailed in paragraph 4(b), Kubient shall be entitled to all fees generated during the termination period regardless of which Party terminates the Agreement, (b) Either Party may terminate this Agreement if the other Party commits a material breach of the Agreement and upon thirty (30) days written notice to the other Party, such other Party hasn't cured the breach within such thirty (30) days. Either Party may terminate the Agreement immediately if the other party (i) becomes insolvent or makes a general assignment for the benefit of creditors;

(ii) suffers or permits the appointment of a conservator or receiver for its business or assets or any similar action by a governmental entity for the purpose of assuming operation or control of the Party due to the financial condition of the Party;

(iii) becomes subject to any proceeding under any bankruptcy or insolvency law whether domestic or foreign and such proceeding or action has not been dismissed within a sixty (60) period; or (iv) has wound up or liquidated its business, voluntarily or otherwise.
(c) Upon termination of the Agreement:
(i) Kubient will cease providing the Services;
(ii) the license granted under section 3 shall be revoked, (iii) Customer will promptly cease use of the Services and the Auction Platform;
(iv) and each Party will return or destroy any of the other Party's Confidential Information then in its possession.

5. Fees and Payment. The Parties agree to share any revenue generated as a result of this Agreement, or Customer's use of the Services or the Auction Platform, as set forth and detailed in each applicable Exhibit. Unless specified otherwise in an Exhibit, Kubient shall be responsible for contracting with all advertisers, agencies, media buyers, and/or sponsors (collectively "Advertisers") on Customer's behalf, including Advertisers with whom Customer has existing relationships. Pursuant to the doctrine of sequential liability, payment from Kubient to Customer shall be made within seven (7) days from Kubient's receipt of payment, regardless of when Customer submits an invoice. Customer acknowledges and agrees that Kubient shall proceed with recovery of the amounts due on a best effort basis but will not initiate any legal action against a delinquent party without the express written consent and support of Customer. Except of taxes associated with Kubient's income, Customer shall be responsible for paying all applicable sales, use or other taxes, duties, or tariffs applicable to its use of the Services.
6. Use of Service.

(a) Customer will comply with all international, federal, state and local laws, rules, and regulations of any governmental or regulating authority ("Law") that are applicable to its business and use of the Service. Customer agrees that it will not transfer or (unless expressly and specifically approved by Kubient in advance and in writing) allow third-party access to the Service. Customer will not modify, translate, alter, tamper with, repair, or otherwise create derivative works of any software included in any Service; reverse engineer, disassemble, or decompile any software or Service or apply any other process or procedure to derive source code of any software included in any Service; or resell, transfer, assign, or use as a service bureau any Service. Customer will ensure that its stories, articles, polls, videos, pictures, photographs, images, broadcasts, and any other type of content (collectively the "Content"), and each of its websites, devices, applications, podcasts, ads, emails, databases or any other types of mediums for which the Service is engaged (collectively the "Properties") contains or is linked to a privacy policy in accordance with applicable Law. Customer shall be responsible and solely liable for all the Content (including without limitation all intellectual property rights therein) and the Properties.

You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Early-termination fee capped at 3 months' fees as the sole liquidated amount.

Delete the Customer-payable LD; if an early-termination fee is unavoidable, cap it at 3 months' fees.

**Finding: compliant** (no redline proposed)

The AUDIT rule is protective — it caps audit rights that bind us. Here there are none to cap:

- Full-text searches for *audit*, *records*, *inspect*, and *verif* returned zero hits.
- A paragraph-by-paragraph read of the agreement's single section confirmed the absence: §5 Fees and Payment (p0023) grants Kubient no examination or true-up right, and the only access-type obligation on AP is §1's cooperation covenant (p0001), which supports service delivery rather than any inspection of AP's books, usage, or systems.

Because Kubient has no audit right whatsoever, the position sits above the preferred standard — there is no frequency, notice, cost-allocation, or system-access exposure requiring constraint. Proposing audit machinery here would manufacture an obligation against our own client, so I left the document untouched.

One item flagged in the rationale for the deal team, but deliberately **not** treated as a deviation under this rule: Impressions are measured solely "as measured by Kubient" (p0009), and the revenue share runs through Exhibits with no AP-side reporting or verification right. An audit right running *in our favor* over Kubient's reporting would benefit us, and belongs under the reporting/revenue-verification rule rather than being redlined here.

You are an independent verifier of one proposed contract finding.
Judge the proposal against the supplied playbook rule, original paragraphs, resolved definitions, deterministic checks, rendered redline, and comment.
Do not rely on hidden drafter reasoning. Fail invalid, directionally wrong, or rule-incomplete edits.
Deterministic checks are heuristics (regular expressions and a changed-character ratio), not verdicts: a failed regex may simply be a phrasing variant, and a high changed-character ratio is acceptable when the rule genuinely requires rewriting the clause (for example replacing a governing-law sentence or deleting a take-or-pay obligation). Weigh them as evidence and decide on substance: does the redline reach the playbook position with the smallest edit that does so, and is the comment accurate?

Fail a deviation finding whose cited clause already meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms (the playbook's classification semantics) — a redline that merely upgrades an acceptable fallback to preferred wording is over-flagging. Rule:
ID: AUDIT
Title: Audit rights against Customer
Kind: parametric
Summary: Audits of our usage must be rare, notified, off-site where possible and at the Vendor's cost.
Severity: medium
Category: audit
Position — preferred:
No more than once per 12 months, on 30 days' written notice, during business hours, by an independent auditor bound by confidentiality, at Vendor's cost unless underpayment exceeds 5 %; no direct access to Customer systems.

Position — fallback:
Once per year on 15 days' notice; Vendor bears cost unless underpayment exceeds 10 %.
Position — walk-away:
Unlimited or unannounced audits, or remote access to Customer systems.
Detection guidance:
Find audit/inspection/verification rights binding Customer; extract frequency, notice, cost allocation, system access.
Redline guidance:
Insert the frequency/notice/cost limits with minimal edits; delete system-access language.

Claimed finding status: compliant

Finding rationale:
The Agreement contains no audit, inspection, records-examination or usage-verification right exercisable against the Customer (AP). Full-text searches for "audit", "records", "inspect" and "verif" return no hits, and a read of every paragraph of the single section confirms it: the fees provision (§5, p0023) creates no examination right, and the only access-related obligation on AP (§1, p0001) is cooperation for Kubient to deliver the Services, not a right to audit AP's books, usage or systems. That outcome is better than the preferred position (annual audits, 30 days' notice, independent auditor, Vendor cost, no system access) because Kubient has no audit right at all, so there is no frequency, notice, cost-allocation or system-access exposure to constrain. No redline is warranted; inserting audit machinery would create an obligation against us that does not currently exist. Separately noted for the deal team (not a deviation under this rule): Impressions are measured solely "as measured by Kubient" (p0009) and revenue share is per Exhibit with no AP-side reporting or verification right — an AP audit right over Kubient's reporting would be beneficial to us and can be raised under the reporting/revenue-verification rule rather than here.

The services provided by Kubient pursuant to each specific engagement by Customer (the "Service" or "Services") shall be set forth and detailed in individual exhibits attached hereto (each an "Exhibit"), which shall be subject to the terms and conditions hereof and be incorporated as part of this Agreement. content.text:
**Repaired finding submitted: compliant** (no redline — none is warranted, so no `propose_redline` call was required or permitted).

What the repair fixed: my first pass located the IP coverage only inferentially, via the "arising out of the Services / Auction Platform" limbs plus the IP *ownership* warranties at p0039–p0040. A further search surfaced **p0033**, which I had under-cited — an express Kubient non-infringement warranty covering the Service *and deliverables* against patent, copyright, trademark, trade secret, publicity and privacy claims.

That converts the IP indemnity from an inference into an express two-step chain:

1. **p0033** — Kubient warrants the Service and deliverables "do not and shall not infringe, misappropriate or violate" any third-party IP right.
2. **p0051 limb (iv)** — Kubient's defence-and-indemnity expressly covers "Kubient's breach of any representation or warranty under this Agreement."

So a third-party infringement claim breaches p0033 and is therefore defended and indemnified — with the broad Services/Auction Platform limbs (p0048–p0049) as an independent route to the same result. The verifier's failed check was indeed a phrasing artefact (no limb is *labelled* "IP infringement"), but the finding now cites the operative language that carries the obligation, with p0033 as the quote.

Everything else stands: covered indemnitees and attorneys' fees (p0047), breach of law (limb (iv) + p0041), data incidents/gross negligence/wilful misconduct (limb (v)), standard procedure with pro-AP late-notice language (p0053–p0055), and no cap because p0027 carves indemnification out of the damages exclusion — making the fallback's 3× fees super-cap unnecessary. AP's own indemnity remains properly narrow, so no walk-away condition exists. The two minor shortfalls (the "best of its knowledge" qualifier on the Creative limb, and AP's slightly wider indemnity) stay in the rationale rather than becoming redlines.

One item outside this rule's scope, flagged for whoever owns dispute resolution: p0028 bars any action brought more than one year after termination, which would compress the practical window for enforcing these indemnities — IP claims often surface later. Worth raising there rather than double-flagging the indemnity here.

messages.content:
Rule:
ID: INDEMN
Title: Indemnification by Vendor
Kind: missing
Summary: Vendor must indemnify Customer for third-party IP claims and its own misconduct; Customer's indemnity stays narrow.
Severity: critical
Category: indemnity
Position — preferred:
Vendor defends and indemnifies Customer (and affiliates) against third-party claims alleging the services or deliverables infringe IP, arising from Vendor's breach of law, data breach caused by Vendor, or gross negligence/wilful misconduct; standard procedure (notice, control, cooperation); Customer's indemnity limited to Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of law.

Position — fallback:
Vendor IP indemnity with usual exclusions (Customer modifications, combinations, specifications) and remedies (procure, modify, replace, refund); Vendor indemnity subject to a super-cap of 3× annual fees.

Position — walk-away:
No Vendor IP indemnity at all, or a one-way Customer indemnity for Vendor's services.
Detection guidance:
Locate indemnification / hold harmless / defence language. Deviation if Vendor indemnity is absent, or only Customer indemnifies, or Vendor's indemnity excludes IP infringement. Presence of a narrow Customer indemnity alone does not satisfy this rule.

Redline guidance:
If absent, insert a Vendor indemnity paragraph after the limitation-of-liability or warranty section (or the last numbered section before "General"). If one-sided, add the Vendor obligation and narrow Customer's.

Model language:
Vendor shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Customer and its affiliates from and against any third-party claim, and all resulting damages, costs and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees), to the extent arising out of (a) an allegation that the Services or Deliverables infringe or misappropriate any intellectual property right; (b) Vendor's breach of applicable law; (c) any unauthorised access to or disclosure of Customer Data caused by Vendor; or (d) Vendor's gross negligence or wilful misconduct.


Claimed finding status: compliant

Finding rationale:
Vendor IP-infringement indemnity IS present, by an express two-part chain rather than a single labelled limb. (1) At p0033 Kubient represents, warrants and covenants that "the Service and any deliverables provided hereunder by Kubient do not and shall not infringe, misappropriate or violate any patent, copyright, trademark, trade secret, publicity, privacy or other rights of any third party". (2) At p0051 limb (iv), Kubient's indemnity expressly covers "Kubient's breach of any representation or warranty under this Agreement". So a third-party claim that the Service or deliverables infringe IP is a breach of p0033 and is therefore defended and indemnified. Independently, p0047-p0049 make Kubient liable for ALL third-party Claims "arising out of or in connection with" the Services and the Auction Platform, which on its face captures infringement allegations without needing the warranty chain, and p0039-p0040 add IP ownership/licence warranties that feed the same limb (iv). The indemnity is therefore at least as broad as the preferred position's IP limb.

The remaining preferred elements are met: Kubient "agrees to indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Customer and its officers, directors, managers, members, agents, and employees" from all third-party Claims including reasonable attorneys' fees (p0047); breach of law is covered via limb (iv) plus the compliance-with-Law warranty (p0041); Vendor-caused data incidents, gross negligence and wilful misconduct are covered by limb (v), the acts or omissions of Kubient or any third party it hires, employs, retains or controls (p0051). Direction is correct on our side: AP's indemnity (p0052) is keyed to its own Content and Properties (including infringement by that Content), unauthorised or inappropriate use, its own breach and its own acts or omissions, with no indemnity running to Kubient in respect of Kubient's Services - so the walk-away scenarios (no Vendor IP indemnity, or a one-way Customer indemnity for Vendor's services) do not arise.

Two minor sub-elements fall short of ideal preferred wording and are recorded here rather than redlined, per the playbook's treatment of minor sub-elements: the Creative limb (p0050) carries a "to the best of its knowledge" qualifier, and AP's indemnity extends slightly beyond Customer-provided content and breach of law to unauthorised use and breach of any representation or warranty. Rule:
ID: AUDIT
Title: Audit rights against Customer
Kind: parametric
Summary: Audits of our usage must be rare, notified, off-site where possible and at the Vendor's cost.
Severity: medium
Category: audit
Position — preferred:
No more than once per 12 months, on 30 days' written notice, during business hours, by an independent auditor bound by confidentiality, at Vendor's cost unless underpayment exceeds 5 %; no direct access to Customer systems.

Position — fallback:
Once per year on 15 days' notice; Vendor bears cost unless underpayment exceeds 10 %.
Position — walk-away:
Unlimited or unannounced audits, or remote access to Customer systems.
Detection guidance:
Find audit/inspection/verification rights binding Customer; extract frequency, notice, cost allocation, system access.
Redline guidance:
Insert the frequency/notice/cost limits with minimal edits; delete system-access language.

content.text: I've reviewed the entire agreement. There is no audit, inspection, records-examination or usage-verification right anywhere in it, and searches for "audit", "records", "inspect" and "verif" return nothing.

input.quote: Customer agrees to provide all reasonable and necessary access, support and cooperation for Kubient to provide the Services in a timely and effective manner.
input.rationale: The Agreement contains no audit, inspection, records-examination or usage-verification right exercisable against the Customer (AP). Full-text searches for "audit", "records", "inspect" and "verif" return no hits, and a read of every paragraph of the single section confirms it: the fees provision (§5, p0023) creates no examination right, and the only access-related obligation on AP (§1, p0001) is cooperation for Kubient to deliver the Services, not a right to audit AP's books, usage or systems. That outcome is better than the preferred position (annual audits, 30 days' notice, independent auditor, Vendor cost, no system access) because Kubient has no audit right at all, so there is no frequency, notice, cost-allocation or system-access exposure to constrain. No redline is warranted; inserting audit machinery would create an obligation against us that does not currently exist. Separately noted for the deal team (not a deviation under this rule): Impressions are measured solely "as measured by Kubient" (p0009) and revenue share is per Exhibit with no AP-side reporting or verification right — an AP audit right over Kubient's reporting would be beneficial to us and can be raised under the reporting/revenue-verification rule rather than here.

content.text:
**Finding: compliant** (no redline proposed)

The AUDIT rule is protective — it caps audit rights that bind us. Here there are none to cap:

- Full-text searches for *audit*, *records*, *inspect*, and *verif* returned zero hits.
- A paragraph-by-paragraph read of the agreement's single section confirmed the absence: §5 Fees and Payment (p0023) grants Kubient no examination or true-up right, and the only access-type obligation on AP is §1's cooperation covenant (p0001), which supports service delivery rather than any inspection of AP's books, usage, or systems.

Because Kubient has no audit right whatsoever, the position sits above the preferred standard — there is no frequency, notice, cost-allocation, or system-access exposure requiring constraint. Proposing audit machinery here would manufacture an obligation against our own client, so I left the document untouched.

One item flagged in the rationale for the deal team, but deliberately **not** treated as a deviation under this rule: Impressions are measured solely "as measured by Kubient" (p0009), and the revenue share runs through Exhibits with no AP-side reporting or verification right. An audit right running *in our favor* over Kubient's reporting would benefit us, and belongs under the reporting/revenue-verification rule rather than being redlined here.

The only ownership-adjacent language is Kubient's warranty at p0040 that it owns the IP in the Service, Auction Platform and "products delivered hereunder", AP's warranty at p0043 that it owns the Content and Properties, and the trademark-only provision at p0065 — none of which allocates ownership of AP's Content, Requests or visitor data as between the Parties, assigns deliverables created for AP, or excludes joint ownership.
